newsitem.title: CHINA: FOCUS - China bank bids to halt rise in bad loans.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - China bank bids to halt rise in bad loans.

text.p: China's state banks, saddled with mountains of bad debt from the days of Stalinist central planning, are setting up systems to ensure new loans are repaid, officials said.

However, a central bank official dismissed on Wednesday a report by a U.S. economic forecasting firm that the burden of debt in China's banking system represented one of the most serious threats to global market stability.
"This is totally groundless," a spokesman for the People's Bank of China said.

After years of being forced to lend money to fit government policy decisions, state-run banks -- such as the Construction Bank of China -- are trying to limit bad loans by beefing up their ability to assess financial risk.
"We are trying to reduce risk in our loans," said Li Wentang, head of the bank's project appraisal department.
"Our key task is to see whether the borrower will be able repay the loan," he said in an interview late on Tuesday. "We play an extremely important role for the bank."
U.S. economic forecast firm DRI/McGraw Hill said on Tuesday that 20-40 percent of the $600 billion in outstanding loans in China's banking sector were non-performing.

The spokesman for the People's Bank of China said only two percent of the total were non-performing. In the past, the bank has estimated 13-14 percent of outstanding loans were non-performing while two-three percent would never be recovered.

China's banks have been trying to shed the mantle of central planning and extend loans on market terms. In the old days, banks were viewed by state policy makers as tools to fund state enterprises with little concern for repayment.
The Construction Bank was one of the first state banks to try to limit lending risk by setting up the forerunner of its appraisal department in 1984 with help from the World Bank.

A key goal was to separate the tasks of lending and evaluating credit risk. The bank has since stepped up training for its corps of credit evaluators, which now boasts nearly 2,500 employees throughout its 44 main branches.
This year the bank reorganised its assessment group and created the project appraisal department, which must approve all major loans for fixed asset investment.

The drive to reduce the threat to the financial system from bad loans won top government support this year when economic tsar Zhu Rongji ordered tougher risk controls and strict guidelines for trimming bad debts.
Construction Bank officials did not estimate their own non-performing loans, but said the bank was probably stronger than other state rivals in terms of asset quality.

"We probably have a lower rate of non-performing loans than other big banks because we started our efforts to strengthen credit evaluation earlier," said Sun Hongxian, chief manager of the project appraisal department.

The department looks at the bank's fixed asset lending -- mainly loans for long-term projects such as electric power plants, roads and oil industry development. Li said about half of the bank's loans were for fixed asset investments.
Although China is trying to create a market economy, the state still helps industries it wants to promote. That plays a key role in deciding whether to extend credit, Li said.
"We look to see whether the state supports the sector we are lending to and whether it is getting any priority treatment," he said.
"We then look to see whether there is a market for the borrower's product and we evaluate the efficiency of the operation."
